Fellowship applications / MSCA-IF 2020

Applying for Marie Skłodowska-Curie Individual Fellowship

By Rohit Shrivastava · 22 December 2021 · 15 min read

A personal guide based on the 2020 Individual Fellowship call.

The Marie Skłodowska-Curie Individual Fellowship (MSCA-IF) was one of the most prestigious funding schemes offered by the European Commission.

MSCA fellowships were established in 1996 as Marie Curie Actions and have been known as Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions since 2014. Their aim is to support researchers’ career development and further training at all career stages. In particular, MSCA-IF aimed to develop the creative and innovative potential of postdoctoral researchers through advanced training and international and intersectoral mobility.

As a postdoc, I felt that continuing in the same lab would give me the time to bring my research to a meaningful conclusion and publish the results. I held a two-year LabEx-EpiGenMed fellowship in France, which allowed me to work on multidisciplinary projects. My next step was to find funding to stay in the lab longer, so I began applying for fellowships such as EMBO and MSCA during my first year.

The MSCA-IF application was the most comprehensive and time-consuming writing exercise I had undertaken. For the call I applied to, the deadline was around September. I recommend starting to write at least three to four months ahead, and looking for a host supervisor at least a year in advance. The application had three main evaluation sections: Excellence (50%), Impact (30%), and Quality and Efficiency of the Implementation (20%). Each section had its own threshold, so the application needed to perform well throughout.

  • Beginning instructions
  • Read the Net4Mobility Handbook thoroughly. I treated it as a guide throughout the writing process.
  • Begin by checking the mobility requirements. For the call discussed here, you could not apply with a host in a country where you had spent more than 12 months in the preceding three years, measured at the deadline.
  • Researcher requirements: Applicants needed at least four years of full-time research experience or a PhD by the deadline.
  • Host lab: You needed a host and supervisor willing to support the application and receive you if the fellowship was awarded. They should also help develop the proposal and mentor your career development. The handbook provided further details.
  • Contact your host institution’s research, innovation, or EU grants office. Some sections require information they hold. They can also review the application, provide feedback, and arrange institutional approval.

Part A. Administrative FormsTo be completed online

  • 1. General information. The PDF notes that this section was not used for evaluation.
  • Acronym: Choose a memorable acronym. In the system I used, changing it required creating a new submission file.
  • Proposal title: Give the title of your research project.
  • Duration: Up to 24 months for the fellowship discussed here.
  • Scientific area: Select the area that best represents the proposed work.
  • Descriptors: Select up to five relevant descriptors from the menu.
  • Keywords: Use terms that accurately describe the proposal. I understood these to help identify suitable reviewers.
  • Abstract: Summarise the problem, proposed work, and expected benefits within 2,000 characters.
  • Declarations: Confirm that everyone involved has approved the application and that the information is accurate and complete.
  • 2. Participants and contacts.
  • Participant legal name: The primary host university or institute.
  • Administrative data: If the host had previously applied for or hosted MSCA fellows, some institutional details could already be available.
  • Departments carrying out the work: Identify the department or lab where you will work.
  • Researcher: Provide your name, date of birth, nationality, contact details, and PhD dates.
  • Place of activity or residence: List the duration and countries of your legal residence or main activity, such as work or study, during the five years before the deadline.
  • Supervisor: Provide their name and contact details.
  • Other contact persons: These are usually staff in the host’s research office.
  • 3. Budget: The country coefficient was already entered in the system. Applicants also indicated eligibility for the family allowance.
  • 4. Ethics: Address relevant issues, such as human participants or cells, embryos, animals, personal data, work involving third countries, health and environmental safety, and dual-use research. Explain how these issues will be managed and include the required approvals or justification.
  • 5. Call-specific questions: Include any planned secondment and its location. The form also asked about data protection and participation in the open research data arrangements.

Part B1

Some tips: Put the acronym and fellowship type in the header of each page of Parts B1 and B2. Add page numbers in the footer, for example “Part B1 – Page x of y”.

The template I used required a font size of at least 11 points, single line spacing, and margins of at least 15 mm. Choose a readable font.

Use charts, diagrams, and figures to explain the project.

Tables can help illustrate information. The instructions allowed 8-point text in tables, but tables could not be used to replace the core narrative merely to save space. If you were asked to remove such tables after submission, the resulting text could push the proposal beyond the page limit.

Define abbreviations before using them. Write clear sentences and use first or third person consistently. Make sections complement one another rather than repeating the same information.

Important: Put information in the correct section. An evaluator may not credit information placed elsewhere. Do not assume that the evaluator knows something because you or your supervisor know it. Give them the information needed to assess your proposal.

Failure to follow the layout requirements could lead to a request to correct the format without changing the text, potentially leaving less room for essential information.

1. Excellence

1.1. Quality and credibility of the research project, including novelty, multidisciplinary approaches, and gender aspects

This is the heart of the proposal. Take time to think it through and discuss it with your supervisor before writing. Start with an introduction to the topic and the knowledge gap or problem. Define the question you will address and explain, in simple terms, how you will approach it. I would put this within the first two paragraphs to engage the evaluator.

Follow with the state of the art. Use separate paragraphs to explain the current understanding of each relevant part of the research area. Preliminary or supporting data can help demonstrate feasibility. I tried to end each paragraph with a clear statement of how my project would move beyond the current state of the art. Finish with a take-home message about what the project will deliver and the basis for the working hypothesis. Insufficient discussion of the background research is a common weakness.

Objectives and overview of the action: Define the broad goal and individual objectives. Each objective can have sub-objectives, supported by work packages. For example, Objective 1 might correspond to WP1. Be realistic about what can be achieved in 24 months. In my view, more than four objectives or six to seven work packages can become difficult to justify. Avoid vague objectives that do not explain how they will advance the research.

Because my project was experimental, I also described the tools, techniques, and specific reagents I would use. For example, I explained that I would monitor stress-granule dynamics using live-cell single-particle tracking. This gave the evaluator a concrete understanding of how the work would be done. This extra section was my choice, included for clarity.

1.1.2. Research methodology and approach

Describe the experimental approach and methods in sufficient detail. I like using a figure to explain the approach. Start with the biological question, then describe the work package developed to address it. Link each objective, sub-objective, work package, and figure clearly. Find a balance: do not fill the section with routine materials and methods, but do not be so vague that the experimental design is unclear.

1.1.3. Originality and innovative aspects of the research programme

Explain what is original about the project, what innovation it offers, and what missing information it will provide. Show which knowledge gaps it addresses and how it will advance the field. A project that simply continues published work without a clear new contribution is unlikely to make a strong case.

1.1.4. Interdisciplinary aspects of the action

Identify the techniques and tools you will use and learn across different disciplines. Explain how they fit together in the project. If you cannot identify the interdisciplinary contribution, discuss it critically with your supervisor. Address weaknesses before submitting.

1.1.5. Gender dimension in the research content

Consider how sex and gender are relevant to the research itself. My project concerned a disease that was more prevalent in males than females, so I highlighted how I would ensure appropriate female representation in the research.

1.2. Quality and appropriateness of the training and the two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and host

Explain the mutually beneficial relationship: how the host will support your development and what skills you will bring to the lab.

1.2.1. Transfer of knowledge to the researcher from the host

Describe the supervisor’s expertise and how the host’s facilities and staff will help you acquire new skills. Cover scientific, management, outreach, and transferable skills, and explain how these support your career.

Scientific skills: Specify the training, who will deliver it, and which facilities you will use. Refer to the relevant details in Part B2. If you plan a secondment, explain what you will learn, who will train you, and how it connects to the work packages.

Transferable skills: These are easily overlooked. Consider project and financial management, intellectual property, teaching, and working effectively in a diverse workplace. Support the plan with practical details.

Outreach skills: Include workshops, symposia, open days, writing, and presentations where relevant.

Independent career development: Explain how your supervisor will mentor you in areas such as project management and student supervision. Discuss the plan with your supervisor and the host’s research office. A common weakness is failing to say who will provide training, how and when it will happen, and how progress will be supervised.

1.2.2. Transfer of knowledge to the host from the researcher

Explain which skills you will bring and how you will share them. Think creatively but realistically. You might introduce collaborators through a symposium or teach a technique that is new to the host. Ask friends and your PhD supervisor for ideas. Do not underestimate this section: explain both what you can transfer and how you will do it.

1.3. Quality of supervision and integration into the team and institution

Explain why the host is particularly suitable, including relevant facilities and complementary research expertise.

1.3.1. Qualifications and experience of the supervisors

Your future supervisor can help identify the most relevant achievements: research leadership, awards, grants, reviewing, and invited talks. Explain how their experience will support your development. Describe the career development plan you have agreed, the skills it addresses, how training will be delivered, and how progress will be reviewed. Identify who will attend review meetings and contribute to mentoring.

1.3.2. Quality of the hosting arrangements

Describe the institution’s experience hosting international and EU-funded fellows, such as EMBO and Marie Curie fellows. Explain its support structures and, where applicable, its HR Excellence in Research recognition and commitment to the European Charter for Researchers and the Code of Conduct for recruitment.

Identify the facilities, training, and team members that will support you. You can refer to Part B2 for detail. Describe lab meetings, departmental seminars, journal clubs, troubleshooting support, an open-door policy, and progress reviews. Mention relevant symposia or international networks. Avoid repeating earlier sections; make the information complementary and cross-reference where helpful. Do not forget practical integration into the host and opportunities for national and international networking.

1.4. Potential of the researcher to reach professional maturity and independence during the fellowship

Use evidence from your experience to show leadership, independent thinking, scientific maturity, a developing network, and transferable skills. Explain how these experiences have prepared you for the proposed project and how the fellowship fits the next step in your career. Refer to the CV in Part B2 rather than repeating it in full.

This section can make or break an application. Be precise about your track record, including publications and conference contributions. Show how your experience connects to the proposed work and how the fellowship will help you become more independent.

There was no single rule for dividing the page allowance. I used about four pages for the experimental sections, 1.1–1.1.5, and completed the rest of Excellence within roughly six pages in total.

Include citations and references in the introduction. For the template I used, references appeared as footnotes on the relevant page and counted towards the ten-page limit.

Use bold, underlining, or restrained background colour to highlight key points. Do not overdo it.

2. Impact

2.1. Enhancing the researcher’s future career prospects after the fellowship

Identify specific skills you will develop and connect the training described in Section 1.2 to your career goals.

  • Scientific capacity: New techniques, wider research networks, publications, writing skills, and improved employability.
  • Leadership: Project and financial management, organising workshops or symposia, and supervising students.
  • Outreach: Teaching, dissemination, public presentations, open days, blogs, and podcasts.
  • Career development: Intellectual property management, contact with industry, identifying an independent research niche, and preparing for competitive grants.

Explain how your work addresses a wider challenge. Keep your goals credible. Do not promise an ERC grant immediately after the fellowship without a convincing basis. Consider opportunities outside academia as well, and make the career plan consistent with the project’s stage of development.

2.2. Quality of the proposed measures to exploit and disseminate the project results

Dissemination: Explain how you will share results, knowledge, methods, and techniques. Consider the host’s dissemination policy, conferences, publications, institutional news, scientific magazines, newsletters, and industry events. Social media can also help share discoveries. Explain how the host and supervisor will support these activities.

Exploitation and intellectual property: If the work could have commercial value, explain how intellectual property will be protected and which patent or technology-transfer services will help. Your supervisor or the host’s commercialisation team can provide details.

Include communication activities in the Gantt chart and specify the target audience. I received useful feedback about publishing open access and reaching readers beyond a narrow specialist field. Do not overlook social media as a way to share scientific news.

2.3. Quality of measures to communicate project activities to different audiences

Communication and public engagement: Describe how you will reach schools, colleges, universities, and the wider public. You might contribute to Researchers’ Night or science days, give talks, or organise demonstrations. Be specific about audiences, institutions, and any arrangements already agreed.

Consider how these activities could interest students in science and introduce them to European research opportunities. Possible activities include online meetings, accessible explanations of results, a project blog, a lab website, or short videos. Develop a credible plan with your supervisor and use the host’s existing outreach opportunities. Remember different audiences, including researchers, children, and adults.

3. Quality and Efficiency of the Implementation

3.1. Coherence and effectiveness of the work plan, including tasks and resources

Explain how you will carry out the project and achieve its objectives. Include work packages, milestones, and deliverables across the two years. I presented this as a table, but a table was not mandatory.

I included separate work packages for management, training and knowledge transfer, and dissemination. You do not need to copy the same layout, but these activities should be covered.

I then added a Gantt chart showing objectives, work packages, timing, the location of each activity, deliverables, and milestones.

3.1.1. Appropriateness of tasks

Justify the time allocated to each objective and work package. Explain which skills or techniques need to be established, who will train you, and the time they will contribute. Include support for data analysis, statistics, or bioinformatics. Describe the supervisor’s contribution to training, progress reviews, career development, and project management.

3.2. Appropriateness of the management structure and procedures, including risk management

Progress monitoring and management: Explain who will review the work and how often. In my plan, this included regular progress meetings and broader performance reviews. Identify other lab members who will provide technical or intellectual advice, and cross-reference Section 1.3 where appropriate.

HR services and research office: Describe practical support, such as induction and health and safety training. Your research office can help with institutional details.

Financial services: Explain how the project’s finances will be administered and who will support you. Institutions have different arrangements, so use your host’s actual procedures.

Technology transfer office: If the project could produce patentable technology, identify the resources and expertise available.

Relocation assistance: Explain support with bank accounts, housing, visas, and health insurance. EURAXESS was one source of support with relocation and related practical issues.

Risks and contingency plans: Identify risks in each work package and explain how you will respond. A realistic contingency plan shows that you have thought carefully about feasibility. Where appropriate, make work packages sufficiently independent that one setback does not jeopardise the entire project. Explain how progress monitoring will identify problems early.

3.3. Appropriateness of the institutional environment and infrastructure

Explain why the host environment supports the project’s success. Cover technical facilities, specialist equipment, training, administrative and financial support, and transferable-skills development. Describe practical access to a workbench, office space, a computer, and scientific literature. Refer to earlier sections where appropriate and keep this section focused rather than repetitive.

Part B24. CV of the Researcher

The application discussed here allowed a five-page CV. Tailor it to support Section 1.4. Include publications and relevant manuscripts under revision or in preparation, making their status clear. List awards, scholarships, fellowships, student supervision, teaching, training, conference posters, presentations, and invited talks. Show how your career has developed, and explain any career breaks.

5. Capacities of the Participating Organisations

Include the participating institutions and legal entities. If an institute belongs to a university, give the university’s name. Include the country, supervisor, and organisation’s role.

6. Beneficiary

Provide a page of information for each host institution.

General description: Introduce the institution, its location, research focus, approximate size, affiliations, and access to shared facilities. Mention relevant awards, major grants, and national or international collaborations.

Academic organisation: State whether each host or partner is academic or industrial. This also applies to a second host.

Role and profile of key people: Describe the supervisor’s relevant achievements, affiliations, grants, EU-funded projects, awards, fellowships, reviewing, and invited presentations. Explain how their expertise will support your project and independent career.

Department: Identify the department where you will work.

Key research facilities, infrastructure, and equipment: List resources relevant to the project, such as imaging, genomics, proteomics, or animal facilities.

Independent research premises: Explain your access to the institution’s facilities.

Previous and current involvement in research and training programmes: Mention relevant completed and ongoing EU projects, fellowships hosted, other funding, patents, and institutional achievements. You can also highlight relevant research publications.

Relevant publications or research and innovation products: Include five relevant publications or patents from the lab.

6. Ethical Aspects

If the research involves animals, human participants, or other ethical issues, explain them here. If ethical approval has already been obtained, include the relevant letter.
